name: Drinking water frequently
lead: Drinking water frequently is a habit recommended in many dry-mouth and breath-care guides as a way to relieve a dry mouth and reduce mouth odour.[2][3] Wikipedia lists water among saliva substitutes but cites no specific trial for it.[1]

Grokipedia advises sipping water every 15 to 30 minutes, noting that large amounts at once give only temporary relief.[2] The Wikipedia halitosis article does not present water as a remedy, though it notes breath is worst on waking because of overnight dryness, and that a 2019 Cochrane review found no strong evidence on which interventions work best.[3]

paras: Saliva flow falls during sleep, and dehydration is a listed cause of dry mouth.[1] Intraoral halitosis is often located at the back of the tongue.[3]
No studies found. A 2017 paper examined pH levels in bottled water relevant to dry mouth.[4]

refs.title: Relieving Dry Mouth: Varying Levels of pH Found in Bottled Water
refs.source: Compendium of Continuing Education in Dentistry

card.summary: Frequent sipping is commonly suggested for dry mouth; no trial evidence on odour was found.

quick.overview:
Drinking water frequently is a common suggestion for dry mouth and morning breath.

No specific trial of water for mouth odour was found in the sources reviewed.
quick.mechanism: Water temporarily moistens the mouth and rinses debris; it does not restore saliva production.
quick.risks: Considered low risk; a 2017 paper noted bottled waters vary in pH.
